title: Historical vs saving faith — bare theoretical assent vs practical applying faith
source_text: LXXXI. Porro ut de singulis istis quae a nobis hactenus exposita fuerunt, & circa quae Scholae Reformatae Doctores varie sentire & loqui videntur, mentem nostram aperiamus, ostendimus ex communi Reformatorum sententia, fidem historicam a fide salvifica & justificante accurate distinguendam esse, & inter utramque magnum esse discrimen. Nempe fidem historicam esse nudum & simplicem assensum praebitum Verbo Dei; profectum quidem a Spiritu Sancto, sed in solo intellectu theoretico inhaerentem, & qui voluntatem & affectus non moveat: Fidem vero salvificam non solum theoreticam mentem illuminare, sed practicam quoque afficere, ac voluntatem & affectus permovére; & quod inde consequens est, eandem salvificam fidem ea quae Verbum Dei docet ad credentis usum referre, & speciatim Dei promissiones credenti applicare: quod non praestat fides historica, siquidem illa quae credit otiose contemplatur, tanquam res ad se nihil attinentes.
pass_a_gloss: Further, that we may open our mind concerning each of those things which have hitherto been set forth by us, and about which the Doctors of the Reformed School seem variously to feel and speak, we show from the common judgment of the Reformers that historical faith is to be accurately distinguished from saving and justifying faith, and that there is a great difference between the two. Namely, that historical faith is a bare and simple assent given to the Word of God; proceeding indeed from the Holy Spirit, but inhering in the theoretical intellect alone, and which does not move the will and affections: but that saving faith not only illuminates the theoretical mind, but also affects the practical, and moves the will and affections; and what follows from that, that the same saving faith refers what the Word of God teaches to the believer's use, and specially applies God's promises to the believer: which historical faith does not perform, inasmuch as it idly contemplates what it believes, as things in no way pertaining to itself.
pass_b_english: Common Reformed judgment: historical faith and saving/justifying faith must be sharply distinguished.
Historical: bare simple assent to God’s Word — from the Spirit, but stuck in theoretical intellect, not moving will or affections.
Saving: lights the mind and moves practice — will and affections; refers the Word to the believer’s use; specially applies God’s promises.
Historical faith only idly contemplates what it believes as if it did not touch him.
